_comment: Polynesian expansion batch 157 - Grey, Polynesian Mythology (1855), ch. 15 'The Emigration of Manaia' (pp. 221-234) and ch. 16 'Hine-moa, the Maiden of Rotorua' (pp. 233-245). Topics 4 founding legends, 8 trickster, 3 heroic tales. All passages are labeled paraphrase.

title.en: The Hook in the Tail of the Fish

region.en: Fishing ground off Manaia's village, Hawaiki (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哈瓦基馬納亞村外漁場（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 15, The Emigration of Manaia (London 1855)

summary.en: While Manaia fishes for his spear-making workmen, they ravish his wife Rongotiki. A fish takes his hook in its tail - the traditional sign that a man's wife is being insulted - and he rows home without a word, ties the fish to a thwart for her to find, and turns his revenge crafty: he asks the offenders to make the spears large and strong, so that when he ambushes them their weapons will be too heavy. In the ambush his unknown last-born son Kahu-kaka-nui leaps out first crying his own name; his wife's incantation Tapuwae weakens the fleeing Tupenu, and the insult is paid for.
summary.zh: 馬納亞出海為造矛工匠捕魚，工匠卻趁機強暴其妻龍戈蒂基。一尾魚上鉤——鉤竟掛在魚尾！按毛利俗信，此兆主妻子受人欺辱。他一言不發收竿回村，將魚繫於船板讓妻子自己明白。報仇之道出奇：他囑工匠把矛造得又大又重——埋伏時敵人的兵器便難以招架。伏擊戰中，素未謀面的幼子卡胡卡卡努伊搶先出擊，自報姓名；其妻誦咒『塔普瓦埃』使逃亡的圖佩努腳軟乏力，恥辱終得清償。

sensitivity.note: Sexual-violence episode summarized, not dramatized; recorded here as the motive of a foundational legend.

passages.text: The cause which led Manaia to come here from Hawaiki was his being very badly treated by a large party of his friends and neighbours whom, according to the usual custom when a chief has any heavy work to be done, he had collected to make his spears for him. One day he determined to have his neighbours all warned to come to a great gathering for the purpose of making spears; the messenger arrived at the place of Tupenu, chief of the tribe living there, who encouraged his people to go in obedience to the message of Manaia. After some time it happened that Manaia felt a wish to go and catch some fish for his workmen, so he went off in his canoe with several of his people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 15 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: After he had been gone for some time the workmen assaulted Rongotiki, the wife of Manaia, without any one knowing what they were doing. All this time Manaia, suspecting nothing, was paddling out to sea, and when he reached the fishing-ground they lay on their paddles. His people soon caught plenty of fish, but he had not even a single bite until at last, as they were on the point of returning, he felt a fish nibbling at his hook and gave a jerk to his line to pull it up; when he got the fish up to the side of the canoe, to his surprise he saw that the hook was not in the mouth of the fish, but fast in its tail - and as this had long been esteemed a sign that your wife was being insulted by somebody, he at once knew how his had been treated by his workmen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 15 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Without waiting a moment longer he told his crew to heave up the anchor and return to the shore; whilst pulling in, he took the fish he had caught, with the hook still fast in its tail, tied it on to one of the thwarts of the canoe, and left it there, in order that when Rongotiki saw it she might know without his telling her that he was aware she had been badly treated. At home she was roasting fern-root and made signs to him by which he might know what had happened; but he knew it already from the manner in which his hook had caught in the tail of the fish. He sent her to fetch the fish, and said, 'That is the fish I meant you to bring, lest you should have said that I did not know what had taken place until you told me.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 15 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Manaia then turned over in his mind various plans for revenging himself, and before the fighting broke out he went to the people who had wronged his wife and told them he hoped they would make the spears large and strong, and not put him off with weak things - a mere piece of deceit, in order that when he attacked them their weapons might be too heavy readily to parry their enemies' blows. He lay in ambush with some of his people and nudged with his elbow his son Tu-ure-nui to rush in and kill the first man of the enemy; but being afraid to go he did not move, and whilst Manaia was encouraging him in vain, another young man, whose father had never been told him by his mother, rushed forward, slew the first of the enemy and cried out, 'The first slain of the enemy belongs to me, to Kahu-kaka-nui, the son of Manaia.' Then for the first time Manaia knew that this young man was his son, his last-born son, and pleased with his courage he loved him very much. The ambush followed the youth and slaughtered them; their chief Tupenu fled by the beach of Pikopikoi-whiti, and Manaia called to his wife Rongotiki to utter incantations to weaken his enemy; she repeated the incantation termed Tapuwae and rendered the flying warrior faint and feeble, so that Manaia rapidly gained on him, caught him, and slew him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 15 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tokomaru and the Dog that Led to Land
title.zh: 托科馬魯號與引路的獵犬

region.en: Tongaporutu to Waitara, Taranaki coast, Aotearoa
region.zh: 紐西蘭塔拉納基海岸湯加波魯圖至懷塔拉

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 15, The Emigration of Manaia (London 1855)

summary.en: Driven from Hawaiki by relentless reprisals, Manaia refits his brother-in-law's canoe Tokomaru and tricks its owner into deep water as a sacrifice to the gods, then sails. Far out, his dog scents land, leaps overboard, and swims ahead howling; the canoe follows through the night and at dawn finds the dog beside a stranded whale. Another canoe lands there first but is beaten in the claim dispute by Manaia's earlier sheds, clearings and whale - until the newcomers produce a sacred place, and Manaia, conceding, coasts on to Taranaki, where the old inhabitants are destroyed and the country left for his descendants, the Ngati-Awa.
summary.zh: 復仇之火迫使馬納亞棄鄉遠走。他修好連襟的托科馬魯號，誘其涉入深水，以之祭神，揚帆出海。茫茫大洋上，獵犬嗅得陸地氣息，跳船在前，吠聲引航；破曉時分，犬立於擱淺巨鯨之側。後到的獨木舟亦抵此地，卻因馬納亞先建的棚屋、墾地與鯨魚而在爭執中落敗——直到對方出示先築的聖壇。馬納亞認輸讓地，沿海岸南行至塔拉納基，誅滅原住民，其子孫即納蒂阿瓦部落。

sensitivity.note: Founding legend includes the destruction of earlier inhabitants, reproduced as the record states it.

passages.text: Their army collected and started to avenge themselves on Manaia and his tribe, and to destroy them; they slew many of them, and continued from time to time to attack them, so that their numbers dwindled away, till at length Manaia began to reflect within himself: 'Ah, my warriors are wasting away, and by and bye perhaps I also shall be slain; rather than let this state of things continue, I had better abandon this country, and, removing to a great distance, seek a new one for myself and my people.' He began to repair a canoe and fit it for sea; the name of the canoe was Tokomaru, and it belonged to his brother-in-law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 15 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the canoe was quite fit for sea they dragged it down to the water and hauled it in until it floated; then they brought down the cargo and stowed it away, and Manaia embarked with his wife, his children and his dependants. Then he said to some of his warriors, 'Let my brother-in-law now be slain as an offering for the gods, that they may prove propitious to this canoe of ours.' So he called to his brother-in-law, who was standing on the shore bidding him farewell: 'I say, wade out to me for one minute, that I may tell you something and take my last farewell, for I am going to part for ever from you.' The poor fellow began to wade out; at first the water hardly covered his ankles, next his knees, at last it came up above his loins, and he said, 'Shove the canoe in a little nearer the shore, I shall be under water directly'; but Manaia answered, 'Wade away, there is no depth of water', and to deceive him better kept pretending to touch the bottom with a stick. At length his feet could no longer touch the bottom, and he found himself swimming close to the canoe; then Manaia seized him by the head, and with one blow of his stone battle-axe clave it, and his brother-in-law perished. Having slain his victim, he caught up his dog which had swum out with its master, lifted it into the canoe, and sailed away to search for a new country for himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 15 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: He sailed on and on, and had proceeded very far from the land they had quitted, when one day the dog scented land and howled loudly, struggling to get loose and jump overboard into the water. The people said, 'We'd better let him go if he wishes it, and see what comes of it'; so they let the dog loose, and he jumped overboard and swam on ahead of the canoe, howling loudly as he went, till night fell, and they could only indistinctly hear the low faint howling; but the dog, after swimming for a long time, finally reached land. The canoe came following straight on the track the dog had taken, and when night ended and day began to break, they again heard the howling of the dog, which had landed close to the stranded carcase of a whale; they pulled eagerly to the shore, and there they landed on this island, on Aotea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 15 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: First they allotted out equally amongst them the whale they had found; but Manaia addressed his men, 'We must now build a house to shelter us, and then we will cut up the whale.' Some of them cried 'Here is the best place for our village', others 'No, no, this is the best place', others further along 'Here, here, this is the best place we have yet seen' - thus all were led to wander a long way along the shore exploring the new country. Now there were some other canoes coming close after the Tokomaru, which presently made the land too, saw the marks on the sand and the sheds and cleared ground, and began to claim each one as his own. They disputed: 'When did you arrive here?' 'A long time ago.' 'And we also arrived a long time ago.' Manaia asked, 'What are the proofs you give to show when you arrived here?' - 'But what proofs have you?' - 'The proof I have to show when I arrived here is a whale of mine which I found upon the beach.' They all returned to the landing-place and inspected the sheds and clearings, but when Manaia demanded their sacred place they went together to see it, and when they saw it, Manaia believed them. He was sorely perplexed and abandoned the part of the country he had first reached, coasting right along the shores from Whangaparaoa, doubling the North Cape, making a direct course to Taranaki and making the land at Tongaporutu, between Parininihi and Mokau; they left the god they worshipped there, whose name was Rakeiora. At the river Mokau they left the stone anchor of their canoe - it is still lying near the mouth of the river on its north side, and the present name of the rock is the Punga-o-Matori. They explored the country to Pukearuhe, forded the river of Onaero, passed the plain of Motunui, and reached the river whose old name Manaia changed, calling it after his son Tu-ure-nui; at Kohutu, at the mouth of the river Waitara, they dwelt, and there they found people living, the native inhabitants of these islands; but Manaia and his party slew them, so that the country was left for himself and for his descendants, and for his tribe and their descendants. Manaia was the ancestor of the Ngati-Awa tribe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 15 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Hine-moa Swims Lake Rotorua by the Sound of the Flute
title.zh: 希內莫阿循笛聲泳渡羅托魯瓦湖

region.en: Lake Rotorua and Mokoia Island, Aotearoa
region.zh: 紐西蘭羅托魯瓦湖與莫科亞島

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 16, Hine-moa, the Maiden of Rotorua (London 1855)

summary.en: The low-born but beloved Tutanekai plays trumpet and pipe on a hillside balcony; across the lake the high-born Hine-moa listens nightly, each having secretly loved the other at the great assemblies. Guarded canoes force her to swim: with six dry gourds as floats she strikes out into the dark, steering only by the music, rests clinging to the sunken stump Hinewhata, and warms herself in the hot spring Waikimihia. Breaking Tutanekai's calabashes of water, she draws him to the bath; found under the ledges, 'as beautiful as the wild white hawk', she becomes his wife, and Tiki is comforted with Tutanekai's sister Tupa.
summary.zh: 出身寒微卻受寵愛的圖塔內凱在山坡高台上吹奏號角與竹笛；湖對岸高貴的希內莫阿夜夜傾聽，二人大會中早已暗生情愫。親友扣留舟船防她私奔，她便以六個乾葫蘆作浮漂，循著樂聲泳渡黑夜中的大湖，途中攀住沉木希內瓦塔歇息，又入溫泉瓦伊基米希亞取暖。她打碎圖塔內凱的水葫蘆，引他前來；熱泉岩下，她如白鷹般綽約起身，結為夫妻，笛友蒂基則娶得圖塔內凱之妹圖帕為慰。

sensitivity.note: Rotorua romance legend; place names (Kaiweka, Waikimihia, Hinewhata) anchored in the text.

passages.text: Rangi-Uru was the mother of a chief called Tutanekai; properly the wife of Whakaue-Kaipapa, the great ancestor of the Ngatiwhakaue tribe, she had at one time run away with a chief named Tuwharetoa, and from this affair sprang Tutanekai, who was an illegitimate child; but finally Whakaue and Rangi-Uru were united again, and Whakaue was very kind indeed to Tutanekai, treating him as if he was his own son, so they grew up on the island of Mokoia, Tutanekai and his elder brothers, until they attained to manhood. Now there reached them a great report of Hine-Moa, that she was a maiden of rare beauty as well as of high rank, for Umukaria was her father and her mother's name was Hine-Marii; and Tutanekai and each of his elder brothers desired to have her as a wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 16 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tutanekai built an elevated balcony on the slope of the hill called Kaiweka. He had contracted a great friendship for a young man named Tiki; they were both fond of music - Tutanekai played on the horn, and Tiki on the pipe - and they used to go up into the balcony and play on their instruments in the night; and in calm evenings the sound of their music was wafted by the gentle land-breeze across the lake to the village at Owhata, where dwelt the beautiful young Hine-Moa, the younger sister of Wahiao. Every night the two friends played in this manner, and Hine-Moa said to herself, 'Ah! that is the music of Tutanekai which I hear.' At the great assemblies of the people they had glanced each at the other, until in the breast of each there grew up a secret passion; Tutanekai could not tell whether he might venture to take her hand, and Hine-Moa's heart said to her, 'If you send one of your female friends to tell him of your love, perhaps he will not be pleased with you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 16 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last Tutanekai sent a messenger to tell of his love, and Hine-Moa said, 'Eh-hu! have we then each loved alike?' They had arranged the time at which Hine-Moa should run away to him, and when the maiden asked what should be the sign, he said, 'A trumpet will be heard sounding every night; it will be I who sound it, beloved - paddle then your canoe to that place.' So always about the middle of the night Tutanekai and his friend Tiki went up into their balcony and played; and Hine-Moa heard them, and desired vastly to paddle to Tutanekai; but her friends, suspecting something, had been careful with the canoes, leaving none afloat, but hauling them all up upon the shore. She reflected in her heart, 'How can I then contrive to cross the lake to the island of Mokoia?' Then soft measures reached her from the horn of Tutanekai, and the young and beautiful chieftainess felt as if an earthquake shook her to make her go to the beloved of her heart. She took six large dry empty gourds as floats, three of them for each side, went out upon the rock named Iri-iri-kapua and threw off her clothes and cast herself into the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 16 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: She reached the stump of a sunken tree which used to stand in the lake, called Hinewhata, clung to it with her hands and rested to take breath; whenever she was exhausted she floated with the current supported by the gourds, and swam on again; but she could not distinguish in which direction she should proceed from the darkness of the night - her only guide was the soft measure from the instrument of Tutanekai, and that was the mark by which she swam straight to Waikimihia, for just above that hot-spring was the village of Tutanekai. At the place where she landed there is a hot-spring separated from the lake only by a narrow ledge of rocks, and Hine-Moa got into it to warm herself, trembling all over from the cold and from modesty at the thought of meeting Tutanekai. He felt thirsty and sent his servant for water; the maiden called out in a gruff voice like that of a man, 'Whom is that water for?' - 'It's for Tutanekai.' - 'Give it here, then.' She drank and purposely broke the calabash; this happened repeatedly, and the enraged Tutanekai threw on some clothes, caught his club and came to the bath, crying, 'Where's that fellow who broke my calabashes?' Hine-Moa knew the voice of the beloved of her heart and hid herself under the overhanging rocks - not a real hiding, but a bashful concealing - whilst he went feeling about along the banks; at last he caught hold of a hand and cried, 'Hollo, who's this?' - 'It's I, Tutanekai.' - 'But who are you?' Then she spoke louder, 'It's I, 'tis Hine-Moa.' He threw garments over her and took her to his house, and thenceforth, according to the ancient laws of the Maori, they were man and wife. When the morning dawned a servant peeping into the house saw four feet, and all the village shouted, 'Oh! here's Hine-Moa, here's Hine-Moa with Tutanekai'; and his jealous elder brothers heard it and said, 'It is not true!' - until they saw her following him from the house. Tiki grieved that his friend had a wife and he none, and Tupa, Tutanekai's young sister, was given to him. The descendants of Hine-Moa and of Tutanekai dwell on the lake of Rotorua to this very day, and never yet have their lips forgotten to repeat tales of the great beauty of their renowned ancestress, and of her swimming over here.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 16 (1855); not verbatim.
